scenarios.title: kubectl apply from a laptop
scenarios.situation: Your team deploys Kubernetes apps by running 'kubectl apply' from engineers' laptops. Last Tuesday two engineers applied different versions within minutes; nobody knows which version is actually running, and there's no record of who changed what.
scenarios.prompt: What GitOps change fixes the auditability problem?
evidence:
kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
registry/app:1.4.2
# git history shows 1.4.1 as latest merged; someone applied 1.4.2 by hand
choices: Make git the single source of truth: all manifests live in a repo, and an agent (ArgoCD/Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster toward the git state — every change is a reviewed commit.
Have engineers announce their kubectl applies in chat so there's a record.
Give only one engineer kubectl access so applies are serialized.
Run 'kubectl apply' from a shared jump host instead of laptops.
scenarios.why: GitOps replaces imperative, untracked applies with declarative desired state in git plus continuous reconciliation — the cluster converges to what's committed, and every change has an author, review, and timestamp. Chat announcements and access restrictions don't create a verifiable record; the jump host just moves the problem.
scenarios.hint: The cluster and git disagree, and there's no log of the change. What if the cluster could only ever match what's committed?

scenarios.title: Drift that nobody noticed
scenarios.situation: Someone scaled a deployment to 10 replicas via kubectl during an incident and never scaled back. Cloud bills rose for a month before anyone noticed the git manifests still said 3.
scenarios.prompt: How does a GitOps agent handle this drift?
evidence:
kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}'
10
grep replicas gitops/apps/web/deploy.yaml
  replicas: 3
choices: The agent detects the difference between live state and git and automatically syncs the cluster back to 3 replicas (or alerts, depending on sync policy), closing the loop without human intervention.
The agent updates the git repo to say 10 replicas so they match.
The agent ignores replica counts because they change at runtime.
You must delete the deployment and let the agent recreate it.
scenarios.why: Continuous reconciliation is the core GitOps loop: detect drift, then converge live state toward desired state (auto-sync) or surface it (manual sync with diff). Git is the source of truth, so the agent corrects the cluster, not the repo. Replica count is exactly the kind of field reconciliation watches.
scenarios.hint: In GitOps, git is the desired state and the cluster is actual state. When they differ, which one changes?

scenarios.title: Fifty apps, one repo, total chaos
scenarios.situation: All 50 microservices' manifests live in one flat GitOps repo directory. Every team's PR touches shared files, merge conflicts are constant, and one bad commit took down twelve apps because the sync applied everything at once.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best structural fix?
evidence:
ls gitops/
app1.yaml app2.yaml ... app50.yaml   # flat, 2000+ lines each team edits
argocd app list | wc -l
1   # one Application syncing everything
choices: Adopt the app-of-apps pattern: a parent Application per team/environment that composes child Applications, with per-app directories, so teams own their sync scope and a bad commit is blast-radius-limited.
Put all 50 apps in one giant Helm chart so there's only one file to review.
Give each app its own cluster so they can't affect each other.
Stop using GitOps and go back to kubectl apply per team.
scenarios.why: App-of-apps hierarchically composes Applications: teams get their own Applications (own sync waves, policies, rollback scope) while a parent bootstraps the set. Blast radius shrinks to the broken app. A mega-chart couples all 50 apps' lifecycles; separate clusters are wildly expensive.
scenarios.hint: The failure mode is one sync scope covering everything. How can you nest scopes so each team owns its own?

scenarios.title: Secrets in the GitOps repo
scenarios.situation: The GitOps repo contains base64-encoded database passwords in Kubernetes Secrets. A new engineer cloned the repo on their first day and now has every credential — base64 is just encoding, not encryption.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct approach for secrets in GitOps?
evidence:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  password: U3VwZXJTZWNyZXQxMjM=   # decodes trivially
choices: Keep only references in git (e.g. ExternalSecrets or Vault Agent) so the cluster fetches real secrets from Vault at runtime — git holds a pointer, never the value.
Encrypt the whole repo with git-crypt so the base64 values are protected.
Use stronger base64 by encoding twice.
Move the Secrets to a private repo that only senior engineers can clone.
scenarios.why: GitOps demands everything in git be safe to share — so secrets must not be in git at all, only references that a cluster-side operator resolves from a real secrets manager (Vault via External Secrets Operator or Vault Agent injector). git-crypt breaks the pull-based model (the agent can't decrypt without keys); a private repo still spreads plaintext secrets to everyone with access.
scenarios.hint: Git history is forever and broadly readable. What belongs in git: the secret, or instructions for fetching it?

scenarios.title: ArgoCD vs Flux for a regulated bank
scenarios.situation: A bank needs GitOps on Kubernetes with strict requirements: every sync must be explicitly approved by a second engineer (four-eyes), full audit of who approved what, and no automatic changes to production — ever.
evidence:
- four-eyes approval on every production change
- immutable audit trail of approvals
- zero automatic mutation of prod
choices: Use manual sync mode (ArgoCD manual sync or Flux with suspended automation): git PRs provide review and the audit trail, and a second engineer triggers each sync explicitly — automation proposes, humans dispose.
Enable auto-sync with self-heal on everything for maximum consistency; approvals slow things down.
Run both ArgoCD and Flux simultaneously so they check each other's work.
Deploy with CI pushing images directly and skip GitOps to keep a human in the loop.
scenarios.why: GitOps tools support manual sync precisely for regulated flows: the PR is the proposal and four-eyes review, the sync is the approved execution, and the tool records who synced what when. Auto-sync would violate the no-automatic-changes rule. CI-push reintroduces the untracked-mutation problem GitOps solves.
scenarios.hint: The requirement is human approval before any production mutation. Which sync mode makes the tool wait for a human?

scenarios.title: Image tags: latest strikes again
scenarios.situation: The GitOps repo pins deployments to image tag 'latest'. ArgoCD shows everything synced and healthy, but production is running a three-week-old image while the registry's 'latest' moved on — and rollbacks are impossible because no one knows which digest ran when.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct image strategy for GitOps?
evidence:
image: registry/app:latest   # in git
# registry/app:latest now points to a different digest than what's running
choices: Pin immutable digests (or semantic version tags) in git and update them via automated image-update PRs (Flux image automation / ArgoCD Image Updater) — every running version is a commit, and rollback is 'git revert'.
Keep 'latest' but make ArgoCD poll the registry continuously so it always deploys the newest.
Tag every build 'latest' and also 'stable' and switch between them manually.
Stop pinning versions and let Kubernetes pull whatever is newest at pod restart.
scenarios.why: Mutable tags break GitOps' core promise: git no longer describes what's running, so diffs lie and rollbacks are guesswork. Immutable references (digests or version tags) updated by automation PRs keep every deployment a reviewed commit — rollback is just reverting the commit. Polling 'latest' makes deployments non-reproducible.
scenarios.hint: The tag moved but git didn't change, so GitOps saw nothing to do. What kind of reference can't move out from under git?

domains.name: GitOps with ArgoCD
domains.summary: Operating GitOps with ArgoCD: install and architecture, Applications and Projects, sync policies and strategies, App of Apps, and progressive delivery hooks. Independent training content; this course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: Git as the Source of Truth
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks what makes the new deployment process 'GitOps' rather than 'CI with extra steps'. The pipeline currently builds images and runs `kubectl apply` from Jenkins.
evidence: Jenkins builds image → kubectl apply → cluster (push-based)
k8s YAML committed after the fact
choices: Declare the entire desired state in Git and let an in-cluster agent (ArgoCD) continuously pull and reconcile toward it — Git becomes the single source of truth, changes are PR-reviewed, and the cluster converges automatically including drift correction
Keep the Jenkins push but commit YAML first; order is what matters
GitOps just means storing YAML in Git; the Jenkins flow already qualifies
Replace Jenkins with a bigger Jenkins
scenarios.why: GitOps = declarative desired state in Git + pull-based reconciliation by an agent + continuous convergence. Push-from-CI leaves the cluster writable from outside and can't self-heal drift. The agent pattern is what makes the repo authoritative.
scenarios.hint: If someone hand-edits the cluster, who puts it back?

scenarios.title: First Contact with ArgoCD
scenarios.situation: ArgoCD is installed but the team can't log in: the docs mention an initial admin password in a Secret, and nobody knows which namespace or secret name.
evidence: kubectl create namespace argocd; kubectl apply -n argocd -f install.yaml
argocd-server pod running; login fails with generated guesses
choices: Read the auto-generated password from `argocd-initial-admin-secret` in the `argocd` namespace (`kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d`), log in as `admin`, then immediately rotate it and set up SSO/RBAC
Reinstall ArgoCD with a custom admin password flag
Exec into the argocd-server pod and reset the password in its local config
Delete the secret; ArgoCD falls back to no-auth mode
scenarios.why: The official install creates `argocd-initial-admin-secret` holding the bootstrap password — it's the documented entry point. Deleting it doesn't disable auth; exec-hacking the server bypasses the intended flow. Rotation + SSO is the day-2 hardening.
scenarios.hint: What did the install manifest create for bootstrapping?

scenarios.title: The App That Won't Stay Synced
scenarios.situation: An ArgoCD Application shows OutOfSync forever: every manual sync is reverted within minutes by an autoscaler changing replica counts.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sync configuration?
choices: Enable `selfHeal: true` so ArgoCD reverts drift — but add an `ignoreDifferences` rule for `replicas` (or sync only the fields you own): the HPA legitimately owns replica count, Git owns the rest
Disable the HPA; GitOps means Git controls everything including replicas
Set sync to manual and have someone click Sync after every HPA change
Delete the Application; HPA and ArgoCD are incompatible
scenarios.why: selfHeal makes the agent the enforcer, but fields owned by other controllers (HPA replicas, autoscaler annotations) must be excluded via ignoreDifferences — otherwise you get a permanent sync war. Manual sync doesn't scale; deleting the app abandons GitOps.
scenarios.hint: Which controller legitimately owns the replica count here?

scenarios.title: Fifty Apps, One Cluster, No Guardrails
scenarios.situation: Every team can now create ArgoCD Applications pointing at any repo and deploying to any namespace — including `kube-system`. Audit flags it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct governance construct?
evidence: all Applications in the default project
team-a app deployed a DaemonSet into kube-system
choices: Create an ArgoCD Project per team with `sourceRepos` restricted to their Git repos and `destinations` restricted to their namespaces/clusters, and require Applications to reference their project
Tell teams to be careful; trust but verify
Run one ArgoCD instance per team to isolate them
Disable Application creation; only admins deploy
scenarios.why: Projects are ArgoCD's tenancy boundary: they scope which repos and destinations an Application may use, plus RBAC roles per project. Per-team instances multiply operational cost; 'be careful' isn't a control.
scenarios.hint: What scopes an Application's allowed sources and destinations?

scenarios.title: Bootstrapping the Bootstrap
scenarios.situation: The platform team manages 40 Applications via YAML in Git but still creates each Application object by hand with `argocd app create`. New services take days to onboard.
evidence: 40 hand-created Applications; onboarding = ticket + manual CLI
choices: Adopt the App of Apps pattern: one parent Application syncs a directory of child Application manifests — onboarding becomes a PR adding a YAML file, fully GitOps
Write a shell script looping `argocd app create`; automation is automation
Use ApplicationSets with a git-directory generator to template the 40 apps from the repo layout
Both the App of Apps pattern and ApplicationSets solve this; pick one and standardize
scenarios.why: Both answers converge: manage Applications declaratively (App of Apps parent, or ApplicationSets generators) so onboarding is a Git PR, not a ticket. A shell loop keeps the imperative step. (Accepting either pattern — the key insight is declarative app management.)
scenarios.hint: How do you create an Application the GitOps way?

scenarios.title: Migrations Before the New Version
scenarios.situation: A release needs a database migration Job to run exactly once *before* the new app version rolls out, and roll back if the migration fails.
scenarios.prompt: How do you order this in ArgoCD?
evidence: plain `kubectl apply` ordering is alphabetical and unreliable
Deployment + migration Job in one Application
choices: Use ArgoCD sync waves (`argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave`) to run the migration Job in an earlier wave, plus a `PreSync` hook with `hook.delete.policy` so the Job is cleaned up; failed hooks block the sync — giving you ordering plus rollback gating
Put the migration in a separate Application and sync it by hand first
Use initContainers for the migration; they always run first
Rely on Helm chart hook annotations; ArgoCD ignores sync waves
scenarios.why: Sync waves give deterministic ordering within one sync operation, and PreSync hooks gate the rollout on the migration's success. initContainers run per-pod-start (wrong lifecycle for one-shot migrations); separate apps reintroduce manual sequencing.
scenarios.hint: What runs before the sync completes, and what happens if it fails?

lessons.title: GitOps — Core concepts
concepts: GitOps makes git the single source of truth: desired state is declared in version control, and an in-cluster agent (ArgoCD, Flux) continuously reconciles live state toward it.
Reconciliation is a loop — observe, diff, sync: drift between git and cluster is detected automatically and either corrected (auto-sync) or surfaced for approval (manual sync).
Pull-based delivery beats push-based: the agent inside the cluster pulls changes, so CI never needs cluster credentials — a major reduction in secret sprawl.
The app-of-apps pattern composes Applications hierarchically, giving each team its own sync scope, policies, and blast radius instead of one giant sync.
Secrets don't belong in git — store references (ExternalSecrets, Vault Agent) and let the cluster resolve real values from a secrets manager at runtime.
Immutable image references (digests or version tags) keep git honest: with mutable tags like 'latest', the repo stops describing what's actually running.

example.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/gitops.git
    path: apps/web
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: web
example.walkthrough: This ArgoCD Application points at the apps/web directory of the gitops repo on main and the web namespace in-cluster. The agent continuously compares the two and syncs differences according to the sync policy.

pitfalls: Common trap: committing Secrets with base64 'encryption' — base64 is encoding; use external secret references.
Common trap: using ':latest' image tags — the repo stops describing reality and rollbacks become impossible.
Common trap: one Application syncing everything — a bad commit has unlimited blast radius; use app-of-apps.
Common trap: CI pushing directly to the cluster alongside GitOps — two writers fight; let the agent be the only writer.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Stand up a GitOps reconciliation loop
labs.objective: Deploy an app via ArgoCD or Flux from git and observe automatic drift correction.
steps: Install ArgoCD (or Flux) on a test cluster and point an Application at a repo directory you control.
Commit a Deployment manifest with replicas: 3 and confirm the app syncs.
Introduce drift manually: 'kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=10'.
Watch the agent detect drift (OutOfSync) and sync back to 3 (or trigger manual sync).
Change replicas to 5 via a git commit and observe the cluster converge without kubectl.

checks.hint: Verify the replica count converged to the git value.

labs.title: Externalize a secret from the GitOps repo
labs.objective: Replace a committed Secret with an ExternalSecret referencing Vault.
steps: Install the External Secrets Operator and configure a Vault-backed SecretStore.
Write the real credential into Vault (KV) — never into git.
Replace the in-repo Secret manifest with an ExternalSecret referencing the Vault path.
Sync and verify the resulting Kubernetes Secret exists with the correct value.
Confirm 'git log' shows no commit ever contained the plaintext credential.

checks.hint: Describe the synced Secret and check its type.

simulations.title: Drift nobody committed
simulations.brief: The GitOps agent reports the payments namespace as 'OutOfSync' — but git is clean and nobody merged today. Someone changed the cluster by hand. Work the drift.

steps.symptom: ArgoCD-style status: payments app OutOfSync. Git log: no merges in 48 hours.
evidence: App: payments. Sync: OutOfSync. Diff: Deployment/payments-api replicas 3 (git) vs 5 (live).
kubectl scale deployment/payments-api --replicas=5 by on-call, 14:12, 'to handle the sale'.
options: The drift is a manual scale — reconcile by updating the git manifest to the intended replica count, not by clicking sync blindly
Click 'Sync' immediately to force the cluster back to 3
Delete the app and let GitOps recreate it
The drift will resolve itself on the next sync cycle
steps.explain: Reconciliation is observe-diff-sync: the diff tells you a human scaled for a real reason (the sale). Update git to declare the intended state — syncing blindly would undo a deliberate, load-driven change and re-create the incident.

steps.symptom: The sale ends tonight. The replica count should return to 3 tomorrow.
evidence: Post-sale: scale back to 3. Owner: on-call. Method: currently 'remember to do it'.
payments-api replicas in git: still 3 (never updated for the sale).
options: Make the temporary change explicit in git (or a scheduled override) with a revert plan — 'remember to do it' is how drift becomes permanent
Leave it at 5 — extra capacity is harmless
Scale it back by hand tomorrow and tell no one
Delete the deployment and recreate it at 3
steps.explain: Git is the single source of truth, including for temporary changes: declare the override in git with its expiry, or schedule the revert. Manual changes with memory-based follow-through are exactly how OutOfSync becomes the permanent state.

steps.symptom: Leadership asks how to stop hand-edits to the cluster entirely.
evidence: 47 engineers hold cluster-admin. 'Everyone needs it for emergencies.'
No policy blocks manual mutation of GitOps-managed namespaces.
options: Remove standing cluster-admin, scope emergency access with expiry, and let the GitOps agent own managed namespaces
Keep cluster-admin for everyone — emergencies need speed
Add a wiki page asking people not to hand-edit
Move the GitOps agent to a different cluster
steps.explain: Pull-based GitOps plus scoped RBAC is the structural fix: the in-cluster agent reconciles, humans propose changes via git, and emergency access is temporary and audited. Forty-seven permanent cluster-admins is not an emergency plan — it's the drift factory.

simulations.debrief: Drift is detected automatically by the reconcile loop — but resolved deliberately: understand why the live state diverged, declare the intended state in git, and remove the standing access that lets drift happen.

simulations.title: The mutable latest tag
simulations.brief: Two clusters run 'the same' manifest from git, but behave differently. Both deploy image api:latest. The tag moved between their sync times. Fix the reference.

steps.symptom: Staging and prod both sync api:latest from the same commit — but run different code.
evidence: api:latest resolved at sync: sha256:aaa1 (built Monday).
api:latest resolved at sync: sha256:bbb2 (built Wednesday). Same git commit.
options: Pin immutable references — digests or version tags — so the manifest describes exactly what each cluster runs
Sync both clusters at the same time so latest resolves identically
This is fine — latest is always the newest code
Stop using staging — it causes confusion
steps.explain: With mutable tags like 'latest', the repo stops describing what's actually running — two syncs of the same commit resolve to different artifacts. Immutable references make the manifest a true statement about the cluster.

steps.symptom: The team pins versions but CI still pushes api:2.4.1 twice — the second build overwrote the first.
evidence: api:2.4.1 pushed Monday (sha256:aaa1), pushed again Wednesday (sha256:bbb2). Tag reassigned.
Rollback to '2.4.1' restored Wednesday's code, not Monday's.
options: Make tags immutable in the registry (or deploy by digest) — a version tag must name one artifact forever
Version tags are just labels — overwriting is normal
Never roll back — always roll forward
Use timestamps in tags so they never collide
steps.explain: A version tag that gets reassigned is a mutable tag wearing a version costume — rollback to '2.4.1' must mean Monday's artifact, deterministically. Immutable tags or digest references make the version a promise, not a suggestion.

steps.symptom: GitOps is configured with auto-sync, and a bad image just auto-deployed to production.
evidence: Automated sync: enabled, prune: true. No health gates.
Bad image (crash loop) synced to prod at 03:12. Auto-sync faithfully deployed the declared state.
options: The declared state was wrong, not the sync: gate what gets declared (CI promotion, image verification) — auto-sync only deploys what's in git
Disable auto-sync — manual sync is safer
Auto-sync is broken — replace the GitOps tool
The bad image is CI's fault, not GitOps' — no action needed
steps.explain: Auto-sync deploys the declared state faithfully — that's its job. The control point is what gets declared: CI promotion gates, image verification, and progressive delivery decide which artifact git may reference. Blaming the sync loop misses the actual gate.

simulations.debrief: Immutable image references keep git honest: digests or pinned version tags, registry immutability, and promotion gates controlling what git may declare. The manifest must be a true statement about the cluster.

simulations.title: Secret committed to git
simulations.brief: The GitOps repo contains a base64'd database password in a manifest. 'It's encoded, not encrypted,' the audit notes. The whole repo is cloned to every engineer's laptop. Fix the secret handling.

steps.symptom: Secret manifest in git: password stored base64-encoded. 40+ clones of the repo exist.
options: Rotate the password immediately, then replace the manifest with a reference resolved at runtime from a secrets manager
It's base64 — that's basically encrypted. Leave it.
Delete the manifest from git history — the clones don't matter
Restrict who can clone the repo
steps.explain: Base64 is encoding, not encryption — every clone holder can decode it in one command. Secrets don't belong in git in any form: rotate now, then store references (ExternalSecrets, Vault Agent) and let the cluster resolve real values at runtime.

steps.symptom: The team proposes SealedSecrets-style encryption: encrypted values committed, decrypted in-cluster.
evidence: 'We encrypt with the cluster key and commit the ciphertext. Git stays the source of truth.'
Key rotation story: unclear. Multi-cluster story: unclear. Audit of who decrypted what: none.
options: Encrypted-in-git is acceptable only with a real key-management and rotation story; otherwise prefer manager references resolved at runtime
Encrypted in git is always wrong — never do it
Encrypted in git is always fine — encryption solves everything
Just use base64 — simpler
steps.explain: Encrypted secrets in git can work, but the security moves to key management: rotation, scope, audit, multi-cluster. Without answers there, it's obfuscation with extra steps. Manager references keep the secret out of git entirely — the simpler invariant to defend.

steps.symptom: CI needs cloud credentials to run Terraform — currently a long-lived key in CI variables.
evidence: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: AKIA... (created 2023, never rotated). Scope: admin.
The GitOps agent runs in-cluster with its own scoped service account.
options: Move to pull-based delivery and short-lived workload identity — CI never holds cluster or cloud credentials
Rotate the CI key yearly — that's sufficient
Scope the key down but keep it long-lived
Put the key in the GitOps repo so it's versioned
steps.explain: Pull-based delivery beats push-based precisely here: the in-cluster agent pulls changes, so CI never needs cluster credentials — a major reduction in secret sprawl. Pair with short-lived workload identity and the 2023 admin key retires permanently.

simulations.debrief: Secrets don't belong in git — encoded, encrypted, or otherwise. Store references, resolve at runtime from a manager, and let pull-based delivery eliminate the credentials CI used to need.

simulations.title: CI holds the cluster keys
simulations.brief: The deploy pipeline pushes to the cluster with a kubeconfig stored in CI variables. The kubeconfig is cluster-admin, 2 years old, and shared across 5 pipelines. Redesign the delivery.

steps.symptom: CI pushes manifests with a 2-year-old cluster-admin kubeconfig shared by 5 pipelines.
evidence: Age: 2 years. Scope: cluster-admin. Shared across: 5 pipelines, 3 teams.
Any of the 5 pipelines can delete any namespace. No audit per pipeline.
options: Switch to pull-based GitOps: the in-cluster agent syncs from git; CI only commits manifests and never touches the cluster
Rotate the kubeconfig — a fresh cluster-admin key fixes it
Give each pipeline its own cluster-admin kubeconfig
Shorten the key's name so it's harder to guess
steps.explain: Pull-based delivery removes the entire credential class: CI writes to git, the agent inside the cluster pulls. No kubeconfig in CI means no 2-year-old cluster-admin key to rotate, scope, or leak — the secret sprawl disappears structurally.

steps.symptom: One pipeline still needs to run database migrations — it genuinely must reach the cluster.
evidence: Job: run migrations pre-deploy. Needs: db access, not cluster-admin.
Today it uses the shared cluster-admin kubeconfig 'because it's there'.
options: Give the migration job its own scoped, short-lived credential limited to what migrations need
Keep using the shared kubeconfig — migrations are trusted
Run migrations by hand from a laptop instead
Skip migrations — the app handles schema drift
steps.explain: The exception proves the pattern: the one job that must reach the cluster gets its own scoped, short-lived credential — not the shared skeleton key. Least privilege applies to automation exactly as it does to humans.

steps.symptom: After the migration to pull-based, deploys feel slower — 'push was instant.'
evidence: Push deploy: 40s. GitOps sync interval: 3min poll. 'It feels broken.'
Webhook from git host to the agent: not configured.
options: Configure the git webhook so pushes trigger near-instant syncs — pull-based with webhooks is as fast as push
Go back to push — speed matters more than security
Reduce the poll interval to 5 seconds
Deploys don't need to be fast
steps.explain: Pull-based doesn't mean slow: a webhook from the git host notifies the agent on push, giving push-like speed with pull-based security. The 3-minute poll is the default, not the design — wire the webhook.

simulations.debrief: Pull-based delivery: the agent inside the cluster pulls from git, CI never holds cluster credentials, and webhooks keep it fast. Exceptions get scoped, short-lived credentials — never the shared skeleton key.

simulations.title: One giant app-of-apps
simulations.brief: The platform team manages all 60 services with a single GitOps application. Every sync touches everything, one team's bad commit blocks all deploys, and nobody can tell who owns what. Decompose it.

steps.symptom: Single GitOps app, 60 services, one sync scope. A bad commit in team A's manifests blocks team B's urgent deploy.
evidence: Applications: 1 ('everything'). Sources: 1 repo, 60 service dirs. Sync failures: block all 60.
Team B's hotfix waited 6 hours for team A's broken manifest to be reverted.
options: Decompose into app-of-apps: a parent app per team/scope, each with its own sync policy and blast radius
Keep one app — the coupling encourages careful commits
Split into 60 separate GitOps installations
Let team B edit team A's manifests to unblock themselves
steps.explain: The app-of-apps pattern composes Applications hierarchically: each team gets its own sync scope, policies, and blast radius under a parent. One giant sync couples 60 teams' fates; hierarchy decouples them while keeping one pane of glass.

steps.symptom: After decomposition, team C's app syncs fine but its service can't reach team D's database.
evidence: NetworkPolicies: none. 'The old monolith app handled networking implicitly.'
Team C: 'It worked when everything was one app!'
options: The decomposition surfaced implicit coupling — define the cross-team contract explicitly (service endpoints, network policy, ownership)
Merge C and D back into one app
Give every app cluster-wide network access
It worked before, so the decomposition is wrong
steps.explain: Decomposition surfaces hidden coupling — that's a feature. The old giant app masked cross-team dependencies; now they become explicit contracts: endpoints, policies, owners. Implicit coupling that 'just worked' is tech debt with a good disguise.

steps.symptom: Each team now wants its own repo, its own sync schedule, its own tool version.
evidence: Team A: own repo. Team B: hourly sync. Team C: different GitOps version.
options: Standardize the platform contract (repo layout, sync policy, versions) and let teams vary inside it — paved road, not 60 snowflakes
Let every team do exactly what it wants — autonomy above all
Force everything identical — no variation allowed
One repo for everyone, no exceptions
steps.explain: App-of-apps gives each team its own scope — inside a platform contract. Total freedom recreates 60 snowflakes a 4-person platform team can't support; total rigidity recreates the monolith. The paved road standardizes the how and frees the what.

simulations.debrief: App-of-apps decomposes the giant sync into hierarchical scopes: each team owns its sync policy and blast radius, hidden coupling becomes explicit contracts, and the platform contract keeps 60 services supportable.

consoleSims.title: Infra change by pull request
consoleSims.brief: GitOps starts with git: propose the Redis cache addition on a branch and open the pull request that the pipeline will plan.

tasks.instruction: Open a PR titled 'Add Redis cache to staging' from infra/add-cache into main.
tasks.hint: Pull requests section: title, base main, head infra/add-cache.

tasks.instruction: Approve PR #2 so the plan stage can run.
tasks.hint: Pull requests section: click Approve on PR #2 (your new PR).

consoleSims.debrief: Every infrastructure change is a pull request: the branch holds the proposal, the PR is the review gate, and approval is what lets automation plan it. Git is the source of truth because git is where changes are debated.

consoleSims.title: Plan on PR, apply on main
consoleSims.brief: Wire the safe Terraform flow: select the staging workspace, rebuild, and approve the gated apply.

tasks.instruction: Set the pipeline variable TF_WORKSPACE to staging.
tasks.hint: Variables section: key TF_WORKSPACE, value staging.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build to run the plan.
tasks.hint: Pipeline section: click Trigger new build.

tasks.instruction: Approve the gated deploy stage to apply.
tasks.hint: Pipeline section: click Approve on the deploy stage.

consoleSims.debrief: Safe GitOps for infrastructure: the workspace is explicit, every build plans, and apply only happens on the gated promotion. The plan output is the change's documentation.

consoleSims.title: Register the GitOps-managed app
consoleSims.brief: Onboard the payments API to the cluster the GitOps way: isolated namespace, pinned immutable image, exposed service.

tasks.instruction: Deploy payments-api (image registry.internal/payments-api:2.4.1, 3 replicas) into payments.
tasks.hint: Deployments section: name, namespace payments, pinned image, 3 replicas.

tasks.instruction: Expose payments-api on port 80 as a ClusterIP service.
tasks.hint: Services section: deployment payments-api, port 80, type ClusterIP.

consoleSims.debrief: GitOps-managed workloads are explicit: their own namespace, immutable image references, declared services. The cluster state reads like the git repo because it is the git repo, reconciled.

consoleSims.title: Review the drift-fix PR
consoleSims.brief: Someone opened PR #1 to fix the replica drift. Review it properly: comment, approve, merge.

tasks.instruction: Add a review comment to PR #1 noting the drift cause.
tasks.hint: Pull requests section: Add comment on PR #1, describe the manual-scale drift.
Pull requests section: click Approve on PR #1.
Pull requests section: click Merge on PR #1.

consoleSims.debrief: Drift fixes go through the same gate as features: reviewed, approved, merged. The reconcile loop then converges the cluster — git stays the single source of truth.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.

Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.

Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.

media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
